section_1.title: The Hook: The Musical Analogy
section_1.content: Introduce the concept that any complex periodic signal is just a 'chord' made of 'pure notes.' Define the Fourier Series as a mathematical way to decompose a complicated wave into simple sine and cosine components.
section_1.example: Visualize a grand piano playing a single chord. The Fourier Series acts like a 'mathematical prism' that splits that chord into its individual, pure frequency notes.

section_2.title: Prerequisite: Orthogonality of Sine/Cosine
section_2.content: Briefly explain the 'Basis' concept. Just as 3D space uses x, y, and z axes, periodic functions use a set of sine/cosine functions as an orthogonal basis. This allows us to measure 'how much' of each frequency exists in the signal.
section_2.example: Imagine trying to describe a position on a map using only North-South and East-West lines. If these lines weren't perpendicular, it would be messy. Sine/cosine functions are the perfect 'grid' for periodic signals.

section_3.title: The Core Formula: Breaking it Down
section_3.content: Present the summation formula: f(t) = a₀/2 + Σ[aₙ cos(nωt) + bₙ sin(nωt)]. Explain that a₀ is the average, and aₙ/bₙ are the 'weights' or amplitudes for each harmonic frequency.
section_3.example: An animation showing a square wave gradually forming as we add more sine waves (n=1, n=3, n=5...). Each wave added makes the shape sharper and more defined.

section_4.title: Calculating the Ingredients: Euler-Fourier Coefficients
section_4.content: Explain how to find the 'weights' (aₙ and bₙ) using integration over one period. Emphasize that these integrals represent the correlation between the target signal and the reference frequency.
section_4.example: A visual 'slider' interface where you change the frequency (n). As you slide through values, the graph shows the signal 'filtering' in or out, like tuning an old-fashioned radio.

section_5.title: Real-World Application: Compression and Noise
section_5.content: Conclude by showing how this theory powers modern technology. By identifying and discarding the 'low-weight' frequencies, we can compress files or clean up noisy data.
section_5.example: Show a digital audio signal from a robotic dog. The raw signal looks like chaotic static, but the Fourier Series highlights a single 'barking frequency' (the signal) vs the background static (noise) that can be easily removed.

        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text("- " + line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):

                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

outline.example: Imagine trying to describe a position on a map using only North-South and East-West lines. If these lines weren't perpendicular, it would be messy. Sine/cosine functions are the perfect 'grid' for periodic signals.

    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = ["Periodic functions form an orthogonal basis.", 
                         "Like a grid, they measure frequency.", 
                         "Sine waves define our coordinate system."]
        self.setup_layout("Prerequisite: Orthogonality of Sine/Cosine", lecture_lines)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Display inner product symbol
        inner_prod = MathTex(r"\langle f, g \rangle = \int_0^T f(t)g(t) dt = 0", color="#FF00FF")
        self.place_in_area(inner_prod, 'A1', 'B6', scale_factor=1.2)
        self.play(Write(inner_prod))
